description: B2's package -> algorithm table. If this package is in the dependency graph, which quantum-relevant primitives does it put there? Moved out of lib/collectors/src/crypto-packages.ts on 2026-08-14 so a data revision needs no code edit (C1's rule) and so check:standards polices its retrievedAt dates (G-14). 1.1.0 (2026-08-16) added the maven, golang, nuget and cargo ecosystems.
criticalCaveat: A lockfile records the fully RESOLVED dependency graph. A package matched here may be a transitive dependency of the build toolchain rather than a library the project's own code calls. This table states what a package implements, never that the customer's code uses it — see the toolchainUbiquity flag and docs/Claude/09-open-gaps.md G-20.
curationRules: The algorithm must be a property of the package, not of how a caller configures it. JWT/JOSE libraries (jsonwebtoken, jose, pyjwt) are deliberately absent: their algorithm is an `alg` value chosen at runtime, so a lockfile entry says nothing about which one is in use. Inferring RSA from jsonwebtoken would manufacture findings, and a wrong value is worse than no value (G-05).
`algorithm` must be a canonicalName in algorithms.json, so algorithm-mapping.ts resolves severity/replacement/standard for it at read time. Asserted in algorithm-mapping.test.ts.

No version-range reasoning. The version a lockfile pins is recorded, but this table has no notion of `implemented from x.y.z` or `vulnerable before x.y.z`. Where a claim is known to be version-dependent it is marked needs-check rather than silently applied to every version — see paramiko/DSA below and G-21.

Every claim carries a citation with a verbatim quote from the package's own documentation. A citation without a quote is the unverified claim G-07/G-08/G-09 punished. Where no such quote could be obtained the claim is `needs-check`, not deleted: the gap being visible is the point.

A *bundle* whose cryptography differs per sub-package is absent for the same reason a JOSE library is. `golang.org/x/crypto` is one Go module holding ssh, ocsp, pkcs12, blake2b, chacha20 and much else; the module path in a go.mod says which module is required, never which package is imported, so no algorithm follows from it. Same for `org.bouncycastle:bcpkix-*` and `bctls-*`, which are format and protocol layers over bcprov rather than algorithm implementations.

This table can only emit an `algorithm` that is a canonicalName in algorithms.json, and there are ten of them: RSA, ECDSA, EdDSA, ECDH, DH, DSA, MD5, SHA-1, AES and AES-ECB. ECDH and DH were one entry until 2026-08-16; G-24 split them because a stated size is a curve order in the first and a modulus in the second, and 2048 means different things in each. Several libraries added in 1.1.0 also ship ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA or ChaCha20. Those are omitted rather than approximated, so an entry here under-reports what a library provides and never over-reports it. Where the omission is material the package's `note` says so.

statusValues.verified: A verbatim quote from the package's own documentation supports the claim, read on `retrievedAt`. It does NOT mean the claim was checked against the specific version a lockfile pins.
statusValues.needs-check: No supporting quote was obtained, or the source contradicts the claim for some versions. Carries no `retrievedAt`, because there is no re-verification date to age out — dating an unverified claim is exactly the failure check:standards cannot see.

dedicated.meaning: The package exists to implement this primitive. Presence implies the primitive is available and almost certainly used.
dedicated.rationale: A lockfile match is two claims of very different strength. That the package is in the dependency graph is near-certain: a lockfile is machine-generated and exactly parsed, with no equivalent of the regex collector's false positives on prose or comments — which is why this tier sits above the regex collector's 0.7. That the algorithm is therefore used follows almost automatically for a single-purpose library: nobody installs node-rsa for anything else.

multi-primitive.meaning: One of several primitives the package offers. Presence proves the library is shipped; which primitive the caller invokes is not visible in a lockfile.
multi-primitive.rationale: For a general-purpose library (cryptography, elliptic, node-forge) the second claim genuinely does not follow — the primitive is available, and which of several the caller actually invokes cannot be read from a lockfile. Neither tier approaches 1.0, which is reserved for evidence that observes the algorithm in operation (a completed TLS handshake), and neither is 0: static presence of a crypto library is real inventory evidence.

K-256) elliptic curve library written in pure Rust with support for ECDSA signing/verification/public-key recovery, Taproot Schnorr signatures as defined in BIP340, Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH), and general-purpose secp256k1 elliptic curve group operations which can be used to implement arbitrary group-based protocols.

algorithms.rationale: One of ECDSA, BIP340 Schnorr and ECDH the crate offers; a lockfile cannot say which the caller invokes.

The quoted sentence names Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman explicitly. Split from the former combined `ECDH/DH` entry on 2026-08-16 (G-24): the two families band a stated size against different tables — a curve order against a modulus.

packages.note: The quote is the README's opening sentence with its inline markdown link brackets removed; the wording is otherwise unaltered.

packages.name: ecdsa

citation.quote: Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) as specified in FIPS 186-4 (Digital Signature Standard).

algorithms.rationale: The crate is the generic ECDSA implementation the curve crates build on. Curve-agnostic by construction, so no key size is claimed.

packages.note: The quote is the README's opening line with its inline markdown link brackets removed. This crate is a transitive dependency of every RustCrypto curve crate (p256, k256, p384, ...), so its presence often reflects a curve crate rather than a direct call — the same reading G-20 warns about for the npm toolchain, and the observation's evidence carries the criticalCaveat that says so.
